title: Wireshark
summary: Capture and read network traffic packet by packet, using sample captures in your browser.

lessons.title: Reading a capture: a web visit

concept.text:
**Wireshark** is a free tool that captures the traffic passing through a network interface and shows every packet in detail. It is how network engineers find out why something is slow or broken, and how security analysts see what really happened.

The window has three panes: the **packet list** (one row per packet), the **packet details** (each protocol layer, expandable) and the raw bytes. The key skill is filtering: a busy network produces thousands of packets a second, and a **display filter** such as `dns` or `ip.addr==10.0.0.5` shows only the ones that matter.
concept.analogy: Wireshark is a slow-motion replay of a conversation between computers. In real time it is a blur, but frame by frame you can see exactly who said what, in what order, and where it went wrong.

visual.caption: Wireshark's detail pane shows the same layers as the OSI model, for a single packet.

layers.name: Internet Protocol
layers.detail: Source and destination IP addresses, TTL

steps.title: Capture
steps.text: In the real tool, choose your network interface and press the blue fin. Only capture on networks you own or are authorised to monitor. The sample below is a recorded visit to a website.

steps.title: Follow the story
steps.text: Read the Info column from the top. An **ARP** request finds the gateway's MAC address. A **DNS** query and response turn the name into an IP. Three **TCP** packets (SYN, SYN-ACK, ACK) open the connection. **TLS** hellos set up encryption. After that, only 'Application Data' is visible.

steps.title: Filter
steps.text: Type a display filter to narrow the list. Combine conditions with `&&`.

steps.title: Spot what stands out
steps.text: Filter for `http`. Packet 13 is an unencrypted login: the username and password are readable by anyone on the path. Then filter for `tcp.port==23` to find a Telnet connection attempt being refused.

packets.note: The PC needs the gateway's MAC address before it can send anything off its own network.
The reply is unicast, straight back to the asker.
DNS uses UDP port 53. The source port is a random ephemeral port.
The answer can be cached for 3600 seconds (its TTL).
Step 1 of the three-way handshake.
Step 2: the server agrees and acknowledges. The 22 ms gap is the round-trip time to the server.
Step 3: connection established.
The server name is visible here even though the rest of the session will be encrypted.

packets.info: Server Hello, Change Cipher Spec, Application Data
packets.note: In TLS 1.3 the certificate is already encrypted, so Wireshark shows it as Application Data.
This is the HTTP request, but all you can see is that it exists and how big it is.
The encrypted response: the web page.
Port 80: this next connection is plain, unencrypted HTTP.
A login over HTTP. The password is in clear text for anyone on the path. Compare this with packets 10 and 11.
The session cookie is also sent in clear text, so it could be stolen and reused.
Something is trying to open Telnet, an insecure legacy protocol.
RST means the port is closed: nothing is listening. Many SYNs to different ports answered by RSTs is the signature of a port scan.

challenge.prompt: Using the sample capture: (1) which display filter shows only the encrypted web session to example.com? (2) What are the username and password in the insecure login, and which packet holds them? (3) How can you tell the Telnet port on 192.168.1.50 is closed?
challenge.hint: Try the `tcp.port==443` and `http` filter buttons, click the packet numbers to inspect them, and look at the TCP flags in the last packet.
challenge.solution:
1. `tcp.port==443` (or `ip.addr==93.184.215.14`) shows packets 5 to 11: the handshake, the TLS hellos and the encrypted application data.

2. **Packet 13**: username `jsmith`, password `Summer2024!`, visible because the form was sent over plain HTTP on port 80.

3. **Packet 16** is a TCP segment with the **RST** flag, sent in immediate reply to the SYN in packet 15. A reset means no service is listening on port 23. An open port would have answered with SYN-ACK.

takeaways: Wireshark shows each packet layer by layer. Display filters find the ones that matter.
A web visit is ARP, DNS, a TCP handshake, a TLS handshake, then encrypted data.
Plain HTTP and Telnet expose credentials. SYN answered by RST means a closed port.

lessons.title: Spotting an attack in a capture

concept.text:
Analysts rarely read captures packet by packet. They look for **patterns** that do not belong: one host talking to many ports, many failed logins, a workstation contacting an address nobody recognises, or large DNS queries with strange names.

This capture records the early stages of an intrusion on a small network: an attacker **scans** a server to find open ports, then tries to get in. Recognising these stages early is what gives defenders time to respond.
concept.analogy: A burglar walks down a street trying every door handle. One attempt means nothing. The pattern, one person and every door within a minute, is what a watchful neighbour notices. A port scan is exactly that pattern on a network.

visual.caption: How a SYN scan reveals port states.
rows: A service is listening. The scanner then sends RST instead of finishing.
The host is up but nothing is listening.
A firewall silently dropped the packet.

steps.title: Find the talker
steps.text: In real Wireshark, **Statistics, Conversations** ranks hosts by traffic. Here, notice that `10.0.0.66` starts every exchange. Apply `ip.src==10.0.0.66`.

steps.title: Recognise the scan
steps.text: Packets 1 to 10: one source, one target, six different destination ports in a few milliseconds. Closed ports answer RST. Ports 22 and 80 answer SYN-ACK, so they are open.

steps.title: See what happens next
steps.text: Filter `tcp.port==22`. After the scan, the same host opens repeated SSH connections seconds apart. Repeated short sessions to an authentication service is the pattern of **password guessing**.

steps.title: Check for the worst case
steps.text: Packet 15 is different: the server itself opens a connection **outbound** to the attacker on port 4444. A server starting a connection to an unknown host on an unusual port suggests a **reverse shell**. This is the moment to isolate the machine.

packets.note: The first of a burst of SYNs to different ports.
Closed.
Open: SSH is listening.
The scanner tears the connection down without completing it: a half-open (SYN) scan.
Closed.
Open: a web server.
No reply at all: filtered by a firewall.
A scripting library, not a normal SSH client, is a hint of automation.

fields: New connection, 1.5 s after the last one

packets.note: A second connection from a new source port.

fields: New connection, 1.5 s after the last one

packets.note: A third. Regular intervals and short sessions suggest a password-guessing tool.
This session lasts much longer than the others. A guess may have succeeded.
The direction has reversed: the server is now calling the attacker. Port 4444 is a common default for reverse shells.
The attacker was listening and accepts the connection.

challenge.prompt: From the capture: (1) which ports on 10.0.0.20 are open, closed and filtered? (2) Which filter isolates the suspected reverse shell? (3) Write a three-line summary of the incident for your team lead.
challenge.hint: Use the reply table above for part 1. For part 2, look for traffic that the server started.
challenge.solution:
1. **Open**: 22 (SSH) and 80 (HTTP), which replied SYN-ACK. **Closed**: 21 and 23, which replied RST. **Filtered**: 3389, which gave no reply.

2. `tcp.port==4444`, or `ip.src==10.0.0.20` to see everything the server initiated.

3. Example summary: "Host 10.0.0.66 port-scanned server 10.0.0.20, then made repeated automated SSH login attempts, one of which appears to have succeeded. About 40 seconds later the server opened an outbound connection to 10.0.0.66 on port 4444, consistent with a reverse shell. Recommend isolating 10.0.0.20 now, blocking 10.0.0.66, preserving logs and resetting all SSH credentials."

takeaways: Look for patterns: one source, many ports, many attempts, or a reversed direction.
SYN scan replies: SYN-ACK is open, RST is closed, silence is filtered.
A server starting a connection to an unknown host on an odd port is a red flag.
